articles.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global disruption that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
articles.summary:
Experts say outage exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.
Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.
“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.
Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.
“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.
The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.
“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.
Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.
Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.
after newsletter promotion
Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.
Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.
In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

articles.title: ASEAN unity faces test as energy crisis, regional conflicts loom over summit
articles.summary: Southeast Asian foreign ministers begin meetings in Manila on Saturday as the regional bloc seeks a coordinated response to surging energy costs, security tensions, and an approaching El Niño,…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 8:51am

MANILA — Southeast Asian foreign ministers begin meetings in Manila on Saturday as the regional bloc seeks a coordinated response to surging energy costs, security tensions, and an approaching El Niño, challenges Philippine President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has said demand collective action.

"Especially at a time when we face multiple crises, from rising oil prices to security concerns and the approaching El Niño, ASEAN needs to act as one," Marcos said ahead of the meetings, which the Philippines will chair. "It is very important that we are united and find plans and solutions to address these problems."

The meetings open a weekend of diplomacy culminating in the November 15 to 17 ASEAN summit, where ASEAN leaders will hold talks with counterparts from major powers including the United States, China and Japan, and discuss wide-ranging issues from the economic fallout from the Middle East conflict, Myanmar, the South China Sea to transboundary pollution.

The gathering comes as the Philippines and other import-dependent Southeast Asian economies grapple with higher fuel costs, which have squeezed households and businesses and added to inflation pressures. The crisis has also exposed the limits of regional energy security, with proposals for a shared oil stockpile still under study.
A summit on the Asia Zero Emission Community, a Japan-led framework that aims to achieve energy security, economic growth and decarbonisation at the same time, will also be held next week.

US President Donald Trump, who will be in Manila for the summit, said this week he was unlikely to order new military strikes on Iran after appeals from countries including Qatar. The comments offered some reassurance to energy markets, though the prospect of renewed military action and disruption to oil supplies remains a concern for fuel-importing countries.
For ordinary Filipinos, the impact of the conflict has been more immediate.
Ahead of the meetings, 50-year-old jeepney driver Lito Albino appealed to Trump to help end the conflict, saying ordinary workers were bearing the consequences of a war they had no part in.

He said the conflict involving Iran had forced him to work longer hours for less money, and with three children and household expenses to cover, higher fuel costs had made it increasingly difficult to support his family.
"No one truly wins in a war. It is the poor and marginalised people like us who suffer the most," Albino said.
Myanmar test
Myanmar will also test ASEAN's ability to maintain a common position on the crisis that has engulfed the country since the military seized power in 2021.

Leaders are expected to review the implementation of the bloc's five-point consensus, its main framework for addressing the crisis, Philippine foreign ministry spokesperson Dominic Xavier Imperial said at a press conference on Friday. Their decision will be reflected in a negotiated document to be issued after the summit.

The South China Sea will feature in discussions with China, with negotiations on a long-delayed Code of Conduct about 70% complete, Imperial said. He said the figure represented overall progress in negotiations, not the proportion of text agreed.

Beyond the diplomatic meetings, Trump's visit is expected to draw protests from workers, students and left-wing groups, calling for an end to the Middle East conflict and the US-led Pax Silica to be scrapped.
Myanmar will also feature in protests planned during the summit, with activists demanding that ASEAN maintain its exclusion of coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing from leaders' meetings.

Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that the United Nations estimates has killed 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

Hlaing's military has received support from China, India and Russia. His administration has gained increasing international recognition in recent months, with some ASEAN countries reengaging and US officials holding secret talks as the Trump administration reverses years of isolation. — Reuters

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Corruption floods Philippine economy
articles.summary: What makes the corruption scandal so damaging is that it has crippled the state’s primary tool for counteracting economic headwinds

blocks.text: The flood-control scandal is no longer simply about questionable contracts, missing dikes, or billions of pesos siphoned from the national treasury. Its economic fallout is now visible across the real economy: public works have ground to a halt, infrastructure spending is contracting, and legitimate builders are drowning in unpaid bills. The Philippines is discovering the hard way that corruption continues to exact a crushing toll long after the stolen cash has vanished.
Corruption inevitably presents two separate bills to the Filipino taxpayer.

The first arrives when public money leaks into inflated project bids, shoddy materials, and ghost drainage structures that exist solely on paper. The second arrives much later, when the bureaucratic machinery seizes up.

Legitimate public works stall, honest contractors wait endlessly for payments, and daily-wage laborers wonder how they will feed their families. The first bill is a brazen theft that sparks moral outrage. The second is a silent administrative breakdown that can steadily undermine an entire national economy.
The Philippines is now confronting that second bill, and the economic data have become impossible to brush aside.

Economic growth slowed to a sluggish 2.1% in the third quarter of 2026, down sharply from 4% a year earlier. Government construction plunged by 15.1%, extending a painful contraction across six straight quarters. Total construction activity slid 4%, while overall capital investment dipped 0.2%. These are not merely abstract figures in an academic report. They reveal an economy losing vital momentum at the precise moment robust public investment should be shielding households from expensive borrowing costs and sluggish consumer demand.

blocks.caption: Source: Philippine Statistics Authority; GDP growth, year on year.

blocks.text: More alarming is the steep contraction documented in the government’s own accounting ledgers.

During the first eight months of 2026, spending on infrastructure and capital outlays fell to P522 billion, down from P798.4 billion during the same period last year. That reflects a massive drop of P276.4 billion, or 34.6%. While overall state disbursements rose, actual capital spending moved sharply in reverse, driven largely by paralyzing bottlenecks within the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

blocks.caption: Source: Department of Budget and Management; first eight months of each year. Decline: P276.4B (34.6%).

blocks.text: That P276.4-billion drop does not represent an estimate of stolen wealth. It simply captures the gap between two periods of state spending. Yet the real-world fallout is severe. Every peso withheld from an honest infrastructure project means cancelled work shifts, idled bulldozers, unpaid hardware suppliers, and delayed improvements to the country’s logistical backbone.

Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan has conceded that bottlenecks in project validation and disbursements have crippled project delivery. These disruptions severely hinder builders from meeting payroll, purchasing supplies, and bidding on new ventures. Lingering governance scandals and institutional uncertainty have chilled investor confidence across the board. (READ: [In This Economy] The Philippines has entered stagflation territory)

Here lies the insidious economic legacy of the flood-control scandal. What began as investigations into specific anomalies has exposed systemic frailties in how the state procures, verifies, and pays for civil works. Government agencies now find themselves attempting to identify irregular contracts while simultaneously trying to keep honest builders solvent.

Consider a reputable contractor who completed an honest road widening or drainage network months ago. He cannot collect his rightful progress billings because state auditors must run endless verification checks on paperwork. His commercial bank does not suspend interest charges while inspectors recheck measurements. His cement supplier still expects timely settlement. His equipment lessor demands payment, and his site workers still need their weekly pay. Eventually, an administrative delay in a regional budget office morphs into an existential cash crunch for an otherwise viable enterprise.

Multiply that predicament across hundreds of general contractors, subcontractors, quarries, steel fabricators, hauling services, and equipment rental firms. The financial damage quickly cascades downward. Small and medium enterprises suffer first and worst because they lack the deep financial reserves required to bankroll state infrastructure out of pocket.

Commercial lenders inevitably inherit part of the damage through non-performing loans, stretched credit facilities, and deteriorated borrower cash flows. While the financial system remains well-capitalized, the transmission mechanism is straightforward: when builders cannot collect from the state, banks face rising credit risks precisely when financing is already tight. (READ: [Vantage Point] Landbank’s P182-million belated retreat)

Legal accountability must proceed. On November 6, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla reported that 79 criminal cases involving flood-control projects valued at roughly P10.78 billion had reached the courts, with charges including plunder, malversation, and anti-graft violations. While that figure reflects total contract values under judicial review rather than verified stolen wealth, the legal reckoning is necessary.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Ombudsman’s presentation on November 6, 2026.

blocks.text: Yet while prosecutors assemble their dossiers, the economy absorbs the blow.

To be fair, corruption did not cause every economic headwind. Elevated power rates, persistent inflation, severe storm damage to agriculture, and high interest rates have all dampened expansion. Headline inflation hit 7.8% in October, while consumer spending rose only 2.4% in the third quarter. These external pressures are genuine.

What makes the governance scandal so damaging is that it has crippled the state’s primary tool for counteracting these headwinds. Rather than injecting vital stimulus and creating local employment, public works programs remain snarled in fear and red tape. Bureaucrats now hesitate to approve routine disbursements lest they face subsequent graft charges, while abandoning oversight would invite renewed pillage.

The Marcos administration must urgently fix this operational impasse. It must establish a clean, swift mechanism to separate clean contracts from fraudulent ones, ensuring that verified work receives payment without delay. Full public disclosure of contract sums, physical progress, and actual disbursements must become mandatory.

The true cost of corruption cannot be measured solely by the assets prosecutors recover or the prison terms handed down. It encompasses idled projects, bankrupt suppliers, lost wages, and squandered opportunities.
The cruelest irony is that ordinary citizens — those who never saw a centavo of illicit gain — are left footing the ultimate bill. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nationwide FAA ground stop: nearly 11,000 flights delayed or canceled at airports across the US
articles.summary: Transportation secretary said stoppage is due to ‘communication issue’ and homeland security says there’s no indication of ‘nefarious attack’

blocks.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights that are due to take off in the US on Friday, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware.

In a post on X, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the stoppage is due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter.
A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.
Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland security director, said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage do not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

blocks.caption: Departure flight screens at Chicago O’Hare international airport on Friday. Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After restoring communications so all airborne flights can land, Mullin said, “we’re going to continue to work to find out what the root of the cause is”.
“We’re not ruling out anything at this point,” Mullin added.
Mullin said the immediate priority was ensuring that planes still in the air would be landing safely, but that there was no clear information on how long the stoppage might last.

In a statement, the Los Angeles mayor, Karen Bass, said that she was aware of the stoppage and receiving updates on it. Los Angeles is home to LAX, the fifth-busiest airport in the US, according to the bureau of transportation statistics.

“I am in close contact with leadership at Los Angeles World Airports (LAWA) to receive real-time updates and assess impacts. We will continue to monitor this evolving situation and work closely with federal and state partners.”

At Ronald Reagan Washington national airport, gate agents, along with most travelers in the terminal, refreshed their phones looking for updates, and attempted to change their flights. Nearly every seat was filled, with some people sitting on the floor and using their luggage as makeshift desks for their laptops.

blocks.caption: Boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport in Washington DC on Friday. Photograph: Zina Desmazes/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway airport and rippled across the rest of the US.
Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.
John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.

A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air. This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 11 September 2001; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.

blocks.caption: Stranded travelers at John F Kennedy international airport in New York City, New York, on Friday. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.
Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

articles.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
articles.summary: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.

blocks.text: ByVictoria Gill
Science correspondent
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.

Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
"He definitely feels lonely," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people

blocks.text: When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people

Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."
King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.
"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo

blocks.text: Image source, Sinead Lynch/The Aspinall Foundation
Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo

African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.
But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.

In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.

It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.
"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.
"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response

blocks.text: Image source, G Forrester
Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response

Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.

The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.
And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".
But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.

No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.
Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.

These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.
The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events

blocks.text: Image source, Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund
Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events
The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.
"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.
And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.
"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives

blocks.text: Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives

Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."

Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."
But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.
Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.
"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."
That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.
"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.
"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

articles.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
articles.summary: The 52-year-old general’s provocative posts and military threats have fuelled rumours of a dynastic succession.

blocks.text: In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.

Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.

The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.

At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".

He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".

Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.
Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.

Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.

"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".

Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.

Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.

Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.

The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.

But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

articles.title: Prosecution miss? Pia Cayetano hits questioning on support for sports
articles.summary: During the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Senator-judge Pia Cayetano expresses 'disdain' over the prosecution's questions for defense witness Chadrin Parian

blocks.text: SENATOR-JUDGE. Senator Pia Cayetano during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Pia Cayetano's Facebook page
During the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Senator-judge Pia Cayetano expresses 'disdain' over the prosecution's questions for defense witness Chadrin Parian

items: During the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Senator Pia Cayetano expressed her disdain towards the prosecution's questioning of a defense witness, Chadrin Parian, regarding a credit card charge incurred by Duterte's husband.

Cayetano defended the importance of supporting young athletes and criticized the notion that public officials should avoid spending on sports due to potential scrutiny, while prosecutors emphasized the need for public officials to avoid ostentatious displays of wealth.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

At the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, an emotional Cayetano took a jab at the prosecution over its line of questioning of a defense witness who is a parent of a young athlete.

Cayetano, an athlete and sports advocate, appeared to take personally the questions of House prosecutor Reynaldo Robles for witness Chadrin Parian, expressing her “disdain” over the line of questioning.
“I will not hide my disdain. I cannot,” Cayetano told Robles.

Parian, whose children belong to the same basketball team as Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, testified during the trial on Thursday, November 12, to explain the P256,000 credit card charge Carpio incurred at a Nike store in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Parian said Carpio had voluntarily offered to pay for the team’s shoes after their international competition.

Robles scrutinized Parian’s explanation, asking whether the witness considered it appropriate for a relative of a public official to spend more than P250,000 on a single purchase, given the constitutional provision directing public officials and their families to lead modest lives.

“My children were 6 and 9 years old when I served my first term as senator. If this happened then, you would impress upon me that, as a law-abiding citizen, I should not put my kids in sports because I will be criticized,” an emotional Cayetano said.

House prosecutors, in separate media interviews, repeatedly clarified that they had no objection to supporting young athletes, stressing that this was not the issue being examined in the impeachment trial.

“That is not the issue. The issue here is our public officials and their relatives should set an example and shy away from what the law calls as ‘ostentatious’ display of wealth, as well as extravagant expenses,” Robles told reporters.

The expenses of public officials, including senators themselves, who support Filipino athletes — including those who end up competing in the Palarong Pambansa, however, hit a sympathetic nerve even among majority senators. Philippine sports, after all, has not been getting a generous share of the budget pie. Was that a miss on the part of the prosecution?

To refocus the questioning, Senator-judge Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri urged the impeachment court to move beyond discussions of credit card expenditures and dwell instead on other substantive issues, including alleged remittances from China to Calle88, a company linked to Duterte.
The credit card purchases are part of lawyer Alex Cabrera’s financial forensic report, which alleged that Duterte and Carpio had accumulated P817 million in undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025.
“Let’s move on and listen to other witnesses that can give us more substantive answers to the case at hand,” said Zubiri.

Cayetano managed to call attention to the plight of Filipino athletes and the need for greater government support, but the impeachment court’s focus is on the allegations against Duterte. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All rescued after cruise ship hit by tanker in New Orleans
articles.summary: The collision leaves 32 people in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for.

blocks.text: Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.
The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".
The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".
"We have zero people unaccounted for which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.

Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told a news conference.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.
Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.
Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.
Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what happened.
Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he saw the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.
"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."
Holford added that he saw passengers and crew members "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.
The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.
Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.

articles.title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
articles.summary:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas

SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on…

blocks.text: SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon, as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket.
Starship Flight 15 is expected to orbit the Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase, in south Texas.
The rocket itself was composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.
SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted and splashed down in the sea. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.
The Starship continued on sailing through space.
SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, as its chief executive Elon Musk pushes his vision of taking humans into space.
More details soon …

articles.title: London, Ont., family raises $500K for daughter's U.S. surgery after being denied funding
articles.summary: A London, Ont., father and daughter who have been fundraising for a major surgery in the United States have now surpassed their goal and are moving ahead with a potentially life-changing procedure…

image.caption: Sydney Gesualdi in 2023, before she was rear-ended at a stop sign leaving her unable to walk. She plans to get surgery in New York early next year. (Submitted by Sydney Gesualdi)

blocks.text: London

A London, Ont., father and daughter who have been fundraising for a major surgery in the United States have now surpassed their goal and are moving ahead with a potentially life-changing procedure that no doctor in Canada would perform.
Sydney Gesualdi is paying out-of-pocket for a surgery she can't get in Canada

After getting rear-ended at a stop sign in 2023, Sydney Gesualdi, now 27, was diagnosed with cranio-cervical instability, a condition involving excessive movement between the skull and the top two vertebrae in the neck, leading to her inability to walk, difficulty breathing, and numbness in her face and limbs.

She was denied spinal consultations by at least eight doctors in Canada, leading the family to consult a neurosurgeon in New York, who recommended cranio-cervical fusion surgery to fuse her skull to her spine—a procedure costing more than $490,000 CAD.
Through a GoFundMe, the family has now raised more than $500,000.
"We're feeling incredibly grateful and a little bit in disbelief," said her father, Joe Gesualdi.

Sydney Gesualdi, now 27, was rear-ended at a red light in July 2023. Since then, she's lost the ability to walk, struggles to breathe and swallow, and experiences extreme fatigue, among other symptoms. (Submitted by Sydney Gesualdi)

Gesualdi started the GoFundMe after the Ontario Ministry of Health denied Sydney's application for full funding through its Out-of-Country Health Services program, leaving the family to raise the money themselves.

items: Desperate to walk again, this 25-year-old Ontario woman is ready to pay $40K for U.S. spinal assessment
London father pushes daughter's wheelchair 200 kilometres to advocate for access to health care

blocks.text: Even after reaching the fundraising goal, people have continued to send in donations, he said, adding that donors are sending money in case the cost changes, or to cover other costs while in the U.S.
Gesualdi said the family is currently in touch with Mount Sinai Hospital in New York and looking at a date in early 2027.
Once the date is finalized, the family will be posting the journey on social media to document it and "show the public where their gifts have gone," he said.
Advocating for change
Along with the fundraising effort, Gesualdi has been working to raise awareness of Sydney's struggle to access treatment in Ontario.

In August, he set out on a six-week, 200-kilometre journey to push her empty wheelchair on foot from London to Queen's Park, stopping along the way to hand out flyers and tell Sydney's story to people he met.
He hoped the walk would also capture the attention of Premier Doug Ford, the Ministry of Health and other decision-makers.
Earlier this week, he and Sydney also met with Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

While they were grateful for the opportunity, he said he expected the ministry would review the out-of-country funding application. He also hoped to discuss their experience in order to improve accessibility to the program.

"We were disappointed to essentially enter the meeting and restate everything that is on the public record to them," Gesualdi said. "Instead of talking about fixes and experiences with the system, we had the system and the way that it works reflected back to us."
"We did request an additional meeting, but there was no commitment to do that."

Joe Gesualdi (left) handing out flyers on his walk to Queen's Park, sharing the details about his daughter Sydney Gesualdi's story and advocating for more accessible out-of-country healthcare treatment. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)
The Ministry of Health said in a statement on Friday that in order to get out-of-country funding approved, a physician must submit a request on behalf of the patient.
"Physicians are responsible for the coordination of health care for their patients," wrote Lily Barnes, the ministry's spokesperson.

"This includes determining the urgency of their patients' need for health services and referrals to other appropriate health care providers and facilities, including referrals outside of province or country."
But that would have required a consultation with a Canadian surgeon, which Sydney could not get.
Gesualdi is now calling for a review of the out-of-country funding program to make it more accessible to other Ontarians dealing with issues like his daughter's.
He believes the process has become too bureaucratic, administered by "career officials" rather than physicians, and that, ultimately, the ministry makes the final decisions itself.
In his view, there are also "a lot of medical assumptions being made in the process," he said, and too few professional opinions being considered.
"The results speak for themselves," he said. "It's continuous denial after denial."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jack joined CBC London after graduating from Fanshawe College in 2025. He previously studied political science and Russian studies at Dalhousie University in Halifax, NS. You can contact him at jack.sutton@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Learning loss report finds COVID-19 school disruptions still impacting students today
articles.summary: A new report says Canadian students are still feeling the impact of the COVID pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with declining achievement — particularly in math — and a discrepancy…

image.caption: A new report says Canadian students are still feeling the impact of the COVID pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with declining achievement — particularly in math — and a discrepancy between standardized test scores and the grades kids receive in class. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

A new report says Canadian students are still feeling the impact of the COVID pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with declining achievement — particularly in math — and a discrepancy between standardized test scores and the grades kids receive in class.
Call for ongoing, evidence-based help to catch up, standardized tests for monitoring

Canadian students are still recovering from the pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with evidence of declining achievement — particularly in math — across jurisdictions, according to a new report.

The report, released Thursday by the Royal Society of Canada, the Canadian Commission for UNESCO and the University of Ottawa, also notes a discrepancy between standardized test scores and the grades kids receive in class

It takes an in-depth look at pandemic learning loss and recovery by examining students' academic results in language arts and mathematics before, during and after COVID-19. Nearly three dozen researchers parsed data from Canadian ministries of education, save Manitoba and Nunavut, which didn't participate.

They analyzed the results of standardized tests, as well as teacher-assigned grades across different grades and — depending on the jurisdiction — considered factors like gender and location (for instance, rural and remote communities versus urban ones).

The pandemic is "going to influence learning for the next few decades and that's not exaggeration," said Tracy Vaillancourt, chair of the report and a professor of education at the University of Ottawa.
"These effects are going to be felt for generations to come."

Findings differed across regions, student populations and grades — not surprising given the varying local contexts across jurisdictions, including how each assesses learning and the patchwork of pandemic approaches taken by each province or territory. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The report is divided by studies of individual provinces and territories, with the findings differing across regions, student populations and grades, said Vaillancourt, who's also the Canada Research Chair in youth mental health and violence prevention.

That's not surprising given the varying local contexts of each jurisdiction, including how each assesses learning, coupled with the patchwork of pandemic responses taken: from how long each closed schools and opted for remote learning to physical distancing in classrooms to recovery efforts implemented afterwards.
Yet across each of the report's individual provincial and territorial studies, there are some broader commonalities, she said:

items: Declines in standardized test results, notably in math. In particular, an emerging gender gap with declining math achievement for girls in several regions and girls' math scores not recovering as quickly as boys have.

A greater impact on younger students, who saw the very building blocks of their foundational knowledge affected — like learning what numbers mean or how to read — versus older students with the basics already established.
A discrepancy between achievement measured by standardized tests, where scores have fallen, versus teacher-administered grades, which rose.

blocks.text: Grade inflation is real, says Vaillancourt, but "this isn't a knock on teachers at all. They were in a really difficult situation" given the high stress of that time.
Teacher grades also tend to incorporate learning progress, she said. High-stakes tests capture a snapshot of student knowledge during one window of time.

During the pandemic, many school systems dropped exams (which never returned in some cases) and asked teachers to weigh assignments differently. Some teachers were directed to reduce content being covered amid the glut of obstacles facing educators and learners alike, ranging from inconsistent or unavailable internet to quarantines to toggling between in-person and online learning.

Researchers also found the pandemic had mixed impacts on reading and writing scores, and that students in some rural, remote and northern communities saw greater declines in overall achievement — and are taking longer to recover — than urban peers.
Taking action

The report lands more than three years after COVID-19 was downgraded from global emergency status. Its authors make several recommendations to governments, starting with support for standardized testing in order to establish reliable, comparable benchmarks of student achievement over time.

items: Canadian teens score well on OECD tests, but sharp drops in reading, math raise concerns

blocks.text: In a time of emergency, "we've got to be compassionate about how kids are faring … but we should also, if possible, monitor what's going on," Vaillancourt said.
"Putting our head in the sand doesn't do anything; it doesn't identify who's most vulnerable [and] how to remedy that vulnerability."

Another recommendation urges the prioritization of evidence-based methods to tackle learning loss — paying particular attention to the most disadvantaged students — and the continual evaluation of whether these initiatives are working.

Tracy Vaillancourt, chair of Canada's pandemic learning loss report, is a professor of education at the University of Ottawa and Canada Research Chair in children's mental health and violence prevention. (Caitlin Taylor/CBC)
COVID worsened existing concerns

The report's findings and recommendations weren't a surprise, since teachers have voiced similar concerns for years, says Clint Johnston, president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation, which represents more than 390,000 teachers and education workers.

"What I see is an exacerbation of a context that honestly already exists in an under-resourced system. We've got children who are falling a bit behind, they're not getting the support they need," he said from Toronto.
"It's not surprising that when there was an interruption, there'd be an impact."
Addressing gaps in student learning requires investment, says Clint Johnston, president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation and a former school teacher. (Jon Hernandez/CBC)
Addressing gaps requires investment, Johnston said, "and right now it essentially seems like we're being asked to make up those gaps — to do more with the same amount — which isn't really feasible."
Montreal parent Katherine Korakakis, whose two kids required tutoring during and after the pandemic, praised the report for validating what parents have long worried about.
"We knew that the pandemic disrupted our children's education, but the questions always were, how significant were those disruptions?"

Katherine Korakakis, president of the English Parents’ Committee Association of Quebec, says the report validates what many parents have seen and been worried about throughout the pandemic. (Matt D'Amours/CBC)

Korakakis, who's president of Quebec's English Parents' Committee Association, backs the report's call to identify students with learning gaps, implement initiatives supporting them and provide continued monitoring.
"Parents need a clear, set plan with meaningful actions and measurable progress," she said.

items: 5 years after COVID-19 started, parents and experts say the impact on kids remains

blocks.text: A final recommendation urges emergency preparedness planners to recognize how detrimental prolonged school closures have been, including affecting kids' broader well-being. Schools are typically where youngsters find social connection, a safe space and myriad supports, including food programs and mental health services.
During emergencies, provided it is safe to do so, "schools should be the last to close and the first to re-open," Vaillancourt said.
She believes initiatives to address pandemic learning loss are required across K-12 into post-secondary and will be for years to come.
We can't think "that because the pandemic feels like it was so long ago, that there's nothing to be done, that the ship has sailed," she said.
"Even though this was in the past, we still have these learners in our system — they're still in my system at the university level — and they still need help."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Jessica Wong covers stories about Canadian school systems and education for CBC News, with a particular interest in how technology impacts the lives and learning of students. Every so often, she revisits her previous life as a journalist covering the arts, entertainment and pop culture. You can email story tips and ideas to jessica.wong@cbc.ca.
With files from Deana Sumanac-Johnson

articles.title: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
articles.summary: A new wave of youth dissent swept India this summer, fuelled by frustration and irreverent online satire.

blocks.text: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissent
ByAzadeh Moshiri
South Asia Correspondent, Delhi
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."

Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.

The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.

In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.

Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.

CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Image
Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.

Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."
